confounds: Diagnosed users had somewhat longer retained timelines on average than controls: approximately 649 versus 530 posts per user, with medians around 408 versus 338; user-level prevalence and raw post shares were therefore both reported.
The dataset is label-imbalanced, with 619 diagnosed and 5,463 control users, and may contain community-specific sampling.
Fandom and identity-related language may proxy age, gender, sexuality, platform subculture, or source selection rather than depression.
Explicit mental-health self-disclosure may be close to the annotation target, so it should not be interpreted as an independent causal or clinical marker.
Rule-based semantic filtering cannot perfectly identify quotation, lyrics, jokes, advocacy, news, or discussion of another person.
Source-order timelines lack reliable timestamps, limiting conclusions about duration, onset, or temporal persistence.
Portuguese social-media spelling, repetition, reply conventions, and topic-specific slang introduce measurement noise.

caveats: Heuristic first-person markers are imperfect and can retain figurative or humorous uses.
Source order lacks timestamps, so persistence is not equivalent to clinical duration.
findings.evidence_summary: The strongest semantic pattern was self-referential and persistent mental-health discussion rather than raw keyword presence. The user-level gap was larger than the raw post-frequency gap, reducing prolific-user distortion.
findings.prompt_guidance: Prioritize user-level prevalence and repeated distinct posts; detect first-person experience and exclude lyrics, jokes, news, advocacy, and discussion of others.

negative_results: Broad relationship, work/study, physical-symptom, and future-orientation vocabulary was common in both labels and was not specific enough alone.
Humor and social-participation terms did not provide a useful stable separator; diagnosed users still showed substantial joking, fandom, and participation language.
Political/news vocabulary had nearly equal user prevalence but higher raw post frequency among controls, with fold-level direction crossing zero.

Isolated depression, suicide, medication, or isolation keywords often occurred in figurative, quoted, lyrical, news, advocacy, or third-person contexts; contextualized repetition was more informative.
